T1: Homeowners will adopt insulation if they receive clear, trusted guidance and can purchase it directly online, because they currently lack awareness and access to suitable products. Who benefits: Kingspan benefits by capturing direct-to-consumer sales and building brand trust.. Why behaviour changes: Awareness and trust overcome the gap between intent and action; direct online purchase removes barriers.. How value is captured: Kingspan sells products at retail margins and earns repeat purchases through its own channel.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to buy insulation online if they trust the brand.; Kingspan can deliver and support consumer orders efficiently.; The online channel can reach homeowners effectively.. Predictions: A landing page with product information and a direct order button will generate at least 5% of visitors purchasing within 12 weeks.; Repeat purchase rate will be at least 15% among visitors who see the product page..

T2: Homeowners will adopt insulation if they receive a financial incentive or a scheme that lowers the upfront cost, because they are price-sensitive and currently lack the capital to purchase. Who benefits: Kingspan benefits by increasing volume through subsidized purchases and building a scheme-based customer base.. Why behaviour changes: A lower upfront cost removes the financial barrier, making the product affordable and attractive.. How value is captured: Kingspan captures value through volume sales of the same product and potential recurring revenue from the scheme.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for quality insulation.; A financial incentive can be delivered at scale without significant additional cost.; The scheme can be managed through Kingspan's existing distribution channels.. Predictions: A scheme offering a discount of at least 15% on a standard product will generate at least 2,000 orders within 12 weeks.; Customers who receive the incentive will have a repeat purchase rate of at least 10% within 6 months..

Test "Direct-to-Consumer vs Incentivized Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online landing page test with two variants: (A) product page with clear DIY guidance and direct purchase option; (B) same page with a simulated discount scheme (15% off) and a call to action to book a free consultation. Visitors are randomly assigned to see either variant.. Sample: 2,000 unique visitors from a panel of UK homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two variants.. Measure: Conversion rate: share of visitors who complete a purchase or book a consultation within 12 weeks.. Predictions: T1: Variant A will achieve a conversion rate of at least 5% among visitors who see it, while variant B will achieve a rate of at least 3% due to the discount's limited impact.; T2: Variant B will achieve a conversion rate of at least 5% among visitors who see it, while variant A will achieve a rate of at least 3% due to the discount's limited impact.. Decision rule: If variant A conversion rate >= 5% and >= 3% points above variant B, proceed with a differentiated DIY consumer proposition (supports T1). If variant B conversion rate >= 5% and >= 3% points above variant A, proceed with a financial incentive scheme (supports T2). If neither threshold is met, do not expand.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners and DIY users, leveraging Kingspan's existing direct-to-consumer channel and clear DIY guidance. The evidence shows homeowners are aware of insulation products and can order online, but they currently lack trust and access. A direct-to-consumer approach with trusted guidance can overcome this barrier and generate demand. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer adoption, trust, or purchase behavior. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual homeowners and DIY users, leveraging Kingspan’s existing direct-to-consumer channel and clear DIY guidance. The evidence shows homeowners are aware of insulation products and can order online, but they currently lack trust and access. A direct-to-consumer approach with trusted guidance can overcome this barrier and generate demand. Target customer: Individual homeowners and DIY users in the UK who are looking to upgrade their homes’ energy efficiency.. Value proposition: Kingspan’s trusted brand and existing direct-to-consumer capability to deliver products and support, combined with clear DIY guidance, create a seamless, trusted path for homeowners to purchase insulation.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Direct-to-Consumer vs Incentivized Purchase Test (2,000 visitors, 12 weeks) to measure conversion rates and decide whether to proceed with a differentiated DIY proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the actual willingness to pay for insulation are uncertain. The test will clarify whether homeowners will purchase through Kingspan’s direct channel and whether trust and guidance are the primary drivers.. Would change if: If the test shows a conversion rate below 5% for the DIY variant, indicating insufficient consumer demand.; If a financial incentive test shows a conversion rate above 5%, suggesting price sensitivity is the primary driver.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a private, convenient, and affordable way to learn a life-saving skill, because they value flexibility and avoid public classes. Who benefits: Individual consumers who want to learn CPR without attending formal classes.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently avoid public classes due to stigma, time constraints, and lack of privacy. A private, home-based solution removes these barriers.. How value is captured: Laerdal can sell kits directly to consumers at a premium price, capture recurring revenue through optional add-ons (e.g., advanced training modules), and build a subscription model for updates.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a private, home-based CPR kit.; The product is easy to use and provides sufficient practice for effective learning.; Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience and privacy benefits.. Predictions: Consumers will purchase a home CPR kit at a price point above the $30 Mini Anne kit.; Purchase intent will be higher among adults who have not taken a formal CPR class.; Repeat purchase or subscription rates will be higher than for a one-time purchase..

T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family-friendly, educational tool that teaches a life-saving skill to children, because parents want to prepare their families for emergencies. Who benefits: Parents of children who want to teach them CPR and other emergency skills.. Why behaviour changes: Parents are increasingly concerned about child safety and want to equip their families with skills that could save lives. A home-based program that involves children makes learning feel like a shared family activity.. How value is captured: Laerdal can sell kits to families at a premium price, offer subscription-based updates for new skills, and bundle with educational content to increase average transaction value.. Assumptions: Parents are willing to invest in home training for their children.; The product can be marketed as a family activity rather than a professional training tool.; The content is age-appropriate and engaging for children.. Predictions: Parents will purchase a home CPR kit for their children at a price point above the $30 Mini Anne kit.; Purchase intent will be higher among parents with children under 12.; Repeat purchase or subscription rates will be higher than for a one-time purchase..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation. Who benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.; Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a health and wellness tool for portion control and carbohydrate counting, because they seek tools that support dietary goals. Who benefits: Individuals following specific diets (e.g., low-carb, keto) and health-conscious consumers.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.; Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%..

Test "Precision vs Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum WTP (EUR) for each scale description.. Predictions: T1: Precision-focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than health-focused group.; T2: Health-focused group will show higher purchase intent and WTP than precision-focused group.. Decision rule: If the average WTP of the precision group exceeds the health group by at least 20% (EUR), recommend developing a precision-focused consumer proposition. If the health group exceeds precision by at least 20%, recommend a health-focused proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), inconclusive and further testing needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a precision-focused consumer proposition for home cooks, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s existing brand reputation for accuracy and direct sales channels. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a precision-focused consumer proposition for home cooks, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s existing brand reputation for accuracy and direct sales channels. Target customer: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.. Value proposition: A precision digital kitchen scale that measures by weight with fraction-of-a-gram accuracy, marketed as the only way to ensure predictable results in cooking.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Precision vs Health Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent for a precision-focused product.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for precision over basic features is unknown; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows the health-focused group achieving a ≥20% higher willingness to pay than the precision group, we would shift focus to a health/portion-control proposition.; If no significant difference is found, we would reconsider the investment or explore other B2B/industrial applications.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Digital Messaging Test: Grant vs Cost‑Effective Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online survey with two parallel messaging groups. Group A sees a message emphasizing government‑approved energy‑efficiency certification and SEAI grant eligibility. Group B sees a message emphasizing long‑term cost savings and reduced future heating bills. Both groups view a product description of Kingspan's 270mm rigid insulation board. Recruit 500 homeowners in the UK who have completed a home energy audit or are considering retrofitting.. Sample: 500 UK homeowners who have completed a home energy audit or are considering retrofitting.. Measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: "Would you purchase this insulation product?" and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, because homeowners are motivated by grant eligibility and government certification.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, because homeowners prioritize long‑term cost savings and energy bill reduction.. Decision rule: If purchase intent for Group A is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A ≥ 65% and Group B ≤ 50%), proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on grant‑eligibility messaging. If Group B is at least 15 percentage points higher, develop a cost‑effective messaging proposition. If neither difference is statistically significant (p ≥ 0.05), do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes government‑approved energy‑efficiency certification and SEAI grant eligibility, rather than a cost‑effective messaging approach. This aligns with the evidence that Kingspan already offers a One Stop Shop service for grant‑eligibility projects and that homeowners are aware of and trust government certification. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes government‑approved energy‑efficiency certification and SEAI grant eligibility, rather than a cost‑effective messaging approach. This aligns with the evidence that Kingspan already offers a One Stop Shop service for grant‑eligibility projects and that homeowners are aware of and trust government certification. Target customer: Homeowners in the UK who have completed a home energy audit or are considering retrofitting, particularly those who are eligible for SEAI grants.. Value proposition: A certified, grant‑eligible insulation product that simplifies the retrofit process and delivers measurable energy‑efficiency savings, positioned as a trusted, government‑approved solution.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to validate purchase intent differences between grant‑eligibility and cost‑effective messaging, using the 15‑percentage‑point threshold.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for certified products and the extent to which homeowners actively seek grants remain uncertain; the test will resolve this.. Would change if: If the test shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two messaging groups (p ≥ 0.05), the recommendation would shift to a cost‑effective proposition.; If new evidence shows that homeowners do not trust government certification or are unlikely to apply for grants, T1 would become less likely and the strategy would need to be adjusted.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Home CPR Device Purchase Intent Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a home CPR training kit description and a time-saving CPR kit description. Sample: 500 adults aged 18-65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to reflect the U.S. population.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and willingness to pay (EUR) for each exposure.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the home CPR kit description compared to the time-saving CPR kit description.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the time-saving CPR kit description compared to the home CPR kit description.. Why behaviour changes: Lack of transparency in water sources and concerns about PFAS, lead, or other contaminants create a need for verification, prompting repeated purchases of test kits.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value by offering repeatable test kits at a premium, leveraging its reputation for accuracy to build a customer base that purchases multiple tests over time.. Assumptions: Homeowners are willing to pay for reassurance about water quality.; Independent testing is perceived as more reliable than utility reports.; Repeat purchases are driven by ongoing uncertainty rather than a single purchase.. Predictions: In a test offering a subscription or multi-test kit, repeat purchase rate will be higher than for a one-time purchase.; Surveyed homeowners will cite uncertainty about water quality as the primary reason for repeat purchases..
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

T1: Homeowners will adopt home insulation as a DIY project when they view it as a low-cost, energy-saving upgrade that can be installed themselves, because they value immediate cost savings and want to improve their home's comfort without major renovations. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking to reduce energy bills and increase home comfort. Why behaviour changes: They perceive insulation as a hands-on, affordable improvement they can complete without professional help, leading them to purchase and install products themselves.. How value is captured: Kingspan captures value through direct-to-consumer sales, premium pricing on quality products, and potential repeat purchases of additional insulation materials.. Assumptions: DIY homeowners have the time, skills, or willingness to learn installation techniques; Consumer perception of cost savings outweighs perceived risk of poor installation; Kingspan's products are accessible and easy to install for DIYers. Predictions: A survey of DIY homeowners will show a higher intent to purchase insulation products than a survey of professional installers; Sales of Kingspan's consumer-facing DIY kits will increase when marketing emphasizes cost savings and simplicity; Customer satisfaction rates for DIY kits will be higher than for professional installation services.

T2: Homeowners will adopt home insulation as a DIY project when they perceive it as a safe, compliant, and legally required upgrade, because they want to avoid fines, meet building regulations, and ensure their home meets energy efficiency standards. Who benefits: Homeowners who are aware of or concerned about building regulations and want to avoid penalties. Why behaviour changes: They choose DIY installation to ensure compliance with local building codes and to avoid potential fines or legal issues associated with non-compliant insulation.. How value is captured: Kingspan captures value through compliance-focused marketing, certification of products for regulatory standards, and potentially higher margins on certified kits.. Assumptions: Regulatory requirements for insulation are clear and enforceable in target markets; DIY homeowners are aware of these requirements and understand the consequences of non-compliance; Kingspan's products can be certified to meet relevant standards. Predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher purchase intent for insulation products when regulatory compliance is highlighted; Sales of certified DIY kits will increase in regions with strict building codes; Customer satisfaction will be higher when products are marketed as compliant and safe.

Test "DIY Home Insulation Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Sample: 500 UK homeowners (200 per condition) recruited via panel, balanced for age, income, and region. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (EUR) for Kingspan's DIY insulation kit. Predictions: T1: Condition 1 (cost savings and simplicity) will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition 2 (regulatory compliance); T2: Condition 2 (regulatory compliance) will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition 1. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition 1 exceeds Condition 2 by at least 10 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing cost savings and simplicity. If the difference is less than 10 points or not significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home insulation) that emphasizes cost savings, simplicity, and DIY capability, supported by evidence of existing consumer reach and market demand for energy-efficient home improvements. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Digital Kitchen Scale Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a digital kitchen scale feature set. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a carbohydrate‑accuracy feature description (supporting T1) or a convenience‑speed feature description (supporting T2). They are then asked about purchase intent on a 7‑point scale and primary reason for choosing the product.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported interest in diabetes management (for T1) and interest in time‑saving kitchen tools (for T2). Randomly assigned to either exposure group.. Measure: Purchase intent score (7‑point scale) and primary reason (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: Group exposed to carbohydrate‑accuracy feature will report purchase intent at least 15 percentage points higher than the control group.; T2: Group exposed to convenience‑speed feature will report purchase intent at least 15 percentage points higher than the control group.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two exposure groups exceeds 15 percentage points, conclude that the corresponding feature (carbohydrate accuracy or convenience) drives higher demand. If the difference is within 15 points, the other feature is equally likely to be the primary driver.. Cost: 12000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation. Who benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.; Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a health and wellness tool for portion control and carbohydrate counting, because they seek tools that support dietary goals. Who benefits: Individuals following specific diets (e.g., low-carb, keto) and health-conscious consumers.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.; Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%..

T1 supports, from mettler-atk-by-weight (independent_study): "Measuring ingredients by weight is the only way to ensure predictable results.". Does not show: It does not show consumer willingness to pay a premium for precision or that they would purchase a differentiated scale..

T2 supports, from mettler-nhs-carb-counting (independent_study): "Weighing foods give you a more accurate measure to work out the carbohydrate content. …". Does not show: It does not show consumer willingness to pay a premium for health-focused features or that they would purchase a differentiated scale..
Looked for evidence against T1: "consumer scales prefer low cost over precision"; found mettler-atk-tolerance, mettler-ar25-ohaus, mettler-atk-precision-need.

T2 neutral, from mettler-atk-by-weight (independent_study): "Measuring ingredients by weight is the only way to ensure predictable results.". Does not show: It does not address consumer motivation for health-focused features or willingness to pay for them..

Test "Precision vs Health Messaging Digital Scale Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants view a product description of a precision digital kitchen scale and a health-focused version. They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 adults (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age and gender to reflect home cooks and health-conscious consumers.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Precision messaging will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than health messaging.; T2: Health messaging will generate higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than precision messaging.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between conditions is at least 10 percentage points, conclude the messaging type drives demand. If the difference is below 10 points, conclude neither messaging significantly influences demand. If willingness to pay is at least 20% above the baseline price, justify a premium; otherwise, no premium is supported.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes precision for accurate ingredient measurement, targeting home cooks and food preparers. Use direct sales channels to capture the premium price justified by precision benefits. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.
The investigation stopped before a recommendation (repeated errors).

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is marketed as a safety necessity and backed by clear regulatory compliance, because they currently lack awareness and trust in CO alarms. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Why behaviour changes: Increased awareness of CO poisoning risks and a trusted recommendation from a medical/safety brand will motivate purchase beyond price sensitivity.. How value is captured: Dräger can charge a premium for a compliant, certified device and capture recurring revenue through accessories and service, leveraging its safety brand credibility.. Predictions: In a test offering a compliant CO detector at a price comparable to non-compliant models, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than for a non-compliant alternative.; Surveyed buyers will cite safety concern as the primary reason for purchase..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home gas detector if it is positioned as a lifestyle accessory or fashion item, because they view safety devices as status symbols rather than purely functional items. Who benefits: Style-conscious consumers who value design and brand identity.. Why behaviour changes: Exposure to design-focused marketing and social proof (e.g., influencer endorsements) shifts perception from utilitarian to aspirational, increasing willingness to pay a premium.. How value is captured: Dräger can command higher prices for design-led products and capture recurring revenue through accessories, limited editions, and brand extensions, leveraging its safety reputation as a design asset.. Assumptions: Consumers associate safety brands with premium aesthetics.; Social media and influencer marketing can effectively influence purchase decisions for non-functional products.; Regulatory compliance can be satisfied without compromising design.. Predictions: In a test offering a design-focused CO detector at a premium price, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than for a functional, low‑priced alternative.; Buyers will cite design and brand appeal as the primary reason for purchase..

Test "Digital Messaging Test for Home Gas Detector" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online ad campaign with two variants: (A) safety-focused messaging emphasizing regulatory compliance, reliability, and home CO risks; (B) lifestyle-focused messaging emphasizing design, status, and brand prestige. Track click-through rate (CTR) and conversion rate (purchase intent) for each variant.. Sample: Estimated 5,000 adult visitors to a consumer safety website, split equally between the two ad variants.. Measure: CTR and conversion rate (purchase intent) for each variant.. Predictions: T1: Safety variant will achieve a CTR of at least 2% and a conversion rate of at least 1.5% among homeowners; lifestyle variant will achieve a CTR of at least 1.5% and a conversion rate of at least 1%.; T2: Lifestyle variant will achieve a CTR of at least 2% and a conversion rate of at least 1.5% among homeowners; safety variant will achieve a CTR of at least 1.5% and a conversion rate of at least 1%.. Decision rule: If the safety variant meets both its CTR and conversion rate thresholds, proceed to develop a safety-focused consumer proposition. If the lifestyle variant meets both its thresholds, develop a lifestyle-focused proposition. If neither variant meets its thresholds, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on B2B markets.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a safety-focused consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) before broader consumer expansion. The evidence shows existing consumer demand for CO alarms and a regulatory environment that allows consumer certification, supporting T1. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a safety-focused consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) before broader consumer expansion. The evidence shows existing consumer demand for CO alarms and a regulatory environment that allows consumer certification, supporting T1. Target customer: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Value proposition: A compliant, reliable home gas detector marketed as a safety necessity, backed by Dräger’s safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed digital messaging test (5,000 visitors, two ad variants) to validate purchase intent for a safety-focused proposition. If thresholds are met, proceed to develop the product; otherwise, focus on B2B markets.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated product are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer certification and competitive response from established consumer brands are also unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows the lifestyle variant achieving its thresholds, we would shift to a lifestyle-focused proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for gas detectors at premium prices, we would reconsider the investment.; If regulatory hurdles or high price sensitivity are identified, we would abandon the consumer expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Proposition Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A (premium‑priced water‑saving version) and Condition B (premium‑priced convenience‑focused version). Each condition presents a mock product description of a professional floor scrubber, highlighting either water‑saving features or convenience and low‑maintenance features. Participants are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay a premium (maximum price they would pay) and to report purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).. Sample: 500 adult consumers in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across both conditions (250 per condition).. Measure: Willingness to pay premium (maximum price) and purchase intent (7‑point scale).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition B because participants prioritize water‑saving features.; T2: Condition B will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than Condition A because participants prioritize convenience and low‑maintenance features.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay premium in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., Condition A: 45% vs Condition B: 35%), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on water‑saving features. If Condition B exceeds Condition A by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience and low‑maintenance features. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes water‑saving and high‑cleanliness features, targeting environmentally conscious homeowners and small‑business owners. Begin with a limited retail launch in regions with high environmental awareness to test demand before broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

The test will resolve whether consumers prioritize environmental benefits or convenience.. Would change if: If the test shows a willingness to pay premium difference of less than 10 percentage points between water‑saving and convenience versions, indicating insufficient demand to justify investment.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for convenience and low‑maintenance features, shifting the recommendation toward a convenience‑focused proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "DIY vs Incentive Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from UK homeowners (n=200) and randomly assigned to one of two messaging conditions: DIY-focused (emphasizing ease, cost savings, and self-installation) or incentive-focused (emphasizing government/local retrofit scheme rebates and deep retrofit benefits). Both conditions include a product description of Kingspan's consumer insulation kit and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question.. Sample: 200 UK homeowners (100 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, home ownership, and region.. Measure: Primary measure: average WTP (in euros) for the Kingspan insulation kit in each condition. Secondary measure: self-reported intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely).. Predictions: T1: DIY condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than incentive condition.; T2: Incentive condition will generate higher average WTP and higher purchase intent than DIY condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP in the DIY condition exceeds the average WTP in the incentive condition by at least €20 (or a 15% increase), proceed to develop a differentiated DIY consumer proposition. If the incentive condition exceeds DIY by at least €20, recommend expanding the existing B2B products into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition. If neither condition exceeds the other by the threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and continue focusing on the current B2B market.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Safety vs Lifestyle Positioning" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Participants view two product concepts for a home gas detector: (A) Safety‑focused version marketed as a medical‑grade, regulatory‑compliant device for CO and gas detection; (B) Lifestyle‑focused version marketed as a design‑led, premium‑priced accessory with aesthetic features. Each concept includes a price point and a brief description. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each concept and state the primary reason for their choice.. Sample: 500 adults in Germany (n = 250 per condition) recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason for choice (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Safety‑focused concept will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent than lifestyle‑focused concept, and safety concern will be the primary reason for purchase.; T2: Lifestyle‑focused concept will achieve at least 20% higher purchase intent than safety‑focused concept, and design/brand appeal will be the primary reason for purchase.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent difference between the two concepts is at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop the higher‑intent proposition. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, consider both concepts but prioritize safety‑focused positioning due to evidence of consumer demand for safety‑branded devices.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance, regulatory certification, and trust in a medical/safety brand. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand for home gas detectors, safety positioning, or lifestyle appeal. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance, regulatory certification, and trust in a medical/safety brand. Begin with a small-scale pilot test to validate purchase intent and primary purchase reason before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters in Germany who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Value proposition: A compliant, certified home gas detector that provides reliable safety monitoring, backed by Dräger’s safety brand credibility, offering peace of mind and potential recurring revenue through accessories and service.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 online choice‑based conjoint survey with 500 German adults to measure purchase intent and primary reason for each concept.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home gas detectors and the willingness to pay a premium for safety‑branded products are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer CO detectors is also unknown.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 10% or if the primary reason for purchase is not safety concern, we would reconsider the safety‑focused approach and explore lifestyle positioning.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for design‑led safety products, we would revise the strategy to prioritize lifestyle positioning.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and choice between two digital kitchen scales: (1) carbohydrate‑accurate digital scale (features precise weight measurement for carbohydrate counting) and (2) convenience‑focused digital scale (features quick-weighing, compact design, and easy-to-use interface). Participants are randomly assigned to view either scale description or both. They are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay (in euros) and likelihood to purchase (1‑10 scale).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported interest in diabetes management or busy household routines.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale) for each participant.. Predictions: T1: Participants viewing the carbohydrate‑accurate scale will report higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than those viewing the convenience scale.; T2: Participants viewing the convenience scale will report higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than those viewing the carbohydrate‑accurate scale.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay for the carbohydrate‑accurate scale exceeds the average willingness to pay for the convenience scale by at least €5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on carbohydrate accuracy. If the difference is less than €5, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Status Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view a product description of a Franke coffee machine (identical specifications) and are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) at three price points: €800, €1,200, and €2,000. They also rate the machine on a 1‑10 scale for premium quality and status appeal. Randomization ensures exposure to premium messaging first, then status messaging, and vice versa.. Sample: 300 UK home consumers (aged 25–45) recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and income levels.. Measure: 1) Average WTP at each price point. 2) Average status rating (1‑10) for the premium messaging condition. 3) Difference in WTP between premium and status messaging conditions.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP at €800 and €1,200 than at €2,000, and higher status rating in the premium messaging condition.; T2: Higher average WTP at €2,000 than at €800 and €1,200, and higher status rating in the status messaging condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP at €800 is at least €100 higher than at €2,000, and the premium messaging condition yields a status rating at least 0.5 points higher than the status messaging condition, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium quality. If the premium messaging condition yields a status rating at least 0.5 points higher than the status messaging condition, proceed with a status‑focused proposition. If neither condition meets its threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, small retail, travel) with unique features and branding.; 2) Expand the existing professional product line into adjacent consumer segments (e.g., add a compact, affordable machine for home use) without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional coffee machines and existing distribution channels.; 4) Partner with or license the professional technology to consumer brands rather than selling under Franke’s own brand..

Searched for "Franke consumer market home coffee machine"; found frankecoffee-mahlkonig-retired, frankecoffee-delonghi-premiumisation, frankecoffee-delonghi-prosumer.

T1: Home consumers are willing to pay a premium for a professional-grade coffee machine that delivers consistent, high-quality brews, and Franke can capture value by selling a differentiated premium product under its own brand rather than through existing channels. Who benefits: Franke benefits by earning higher margins on a premium product and building brand loyalty among prosumers.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly view coffee as a lifestyle product and are willing to invest in equipment that meets professional standards for taste and reliability.. How value is captured: Franke can price the product at a premium, sell it directly through its own channels, and retain control over brand positioning and customer experience.. Assumptions: There is a measurable segment of home consumers who currently use or would switch to a professional-grade coffee machine.; Franke can differentiate its product through Swiss engineering and brand positioning.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for consistent coffee quality over lower-cost alternatives.. Predictions: A survey of target home consumers would show at least 30% indicating they would purchase a professional-grade coffee machine at a price 20% above a standard consumer machine.; Sales of a differentiated premium product would generate higher average revenue per unit compared to a standard consumer machine.; Brand perception surveys would rank Franke as a premium brand among prosumers..

T2: Home consumers are not willing to pay a premium for professional-grade coffee machines because they perceive them as too complex, expensive, or not suitable for their lifestyle, and Franke would not capture value by selling a differentiated consumer product. Who benefits: Franke would not benefit from a premium consumer product; instead, it would face higher development and marketing costs without a guaranteed return on investment.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers prioritize ease of use, affordability, and versatility for their daily coffee needs, and are unlikely to switch to a machine that requires professional-level skill or maintenance.. How value is captured: Franke would not capture value from a consumer product; any value would come from its professional machine line, which already serves the market it aims to serve.. Assumptions: There is a significant segment of home consumers who currently use or would switch to a professional-grade coffee machine.; Franke's current professional machines are already widely adopted and trusted by consumers.; Consumers are price-sensitive and prefer lower-cost alternatives for daily use.. Predictions: A survey of target home consumers would show less than 20% indicating they would purchase a professional-grade coffee machine at a price 20% above a standard consumer machine.; Sales of a differentiated premium product would be low or zero, indicating limited consumer demand.; Brand perception surveys would rank Franke as a premium brand among home consumers, but not as a preferred choice for daily use..

T1 supports, from frankecoffee-delonghi-premiumisation (independent_study): "growing premiumisation among home consumers". Does not show: It does not show that Franke's specific product would be purchased or that consumers would pay a premium price..

T2 supports, from frankecoffee-mahlkonig-retired (independent_study): "the company announced that its previous consumer-oriented machine with flat 54-millimeter burrs, the Mahlkönig Vario Home, would be retired from the product line.". Does not show: It does not show that consumers would not pay a premium for a professional-grade machine, only that Franke previously tried a consumer product that was not successful..

Looked for evidence against T1: "Franke consumer market home coffee machine low demand premium"; found frankecoffee-delonghi-premiumisation, frankecoffee-mahlkonig-retired, frankecoffee-delonghi-prosumer.

Test "Premium vs. Standard Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home coffee consumers (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Premium positioning - professional-grade machine with Swiss engineering, consistent brews, and premium price; (B) Standard positioning - compact, affordable machine for daily use, emphasizing ease of use and versatility. Both conditions present the same product (Franke A300) at a price point 20% above a standard consumer machine.. Sample: 300 home coffee consumers recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and coffee consumption frequency.. Measure: Percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the product at the premium price (Condition A) versus the standard price (Condition B).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants in Condition A will indicate purchase at the premium price, indicating demand for a differentiated premium proposition.; T2: Less than 20% of participants in Condition A will indicate purchase at the premium price, indicating that consumers are not willing to pay a premium for professional-grade machines.. Decision rule: If the premium purchase rate in Condition A is at least 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If the premium purchase rate is below 20%, do not invest in a differentiated consumer product and focus on the existing professional line.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated premium consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home office, travel) rather than a broad consumer expansion. The evidence shows growing premiumisation among home consumers and Franke’s existing professional machines are already trusted by prosumers, so a premium positioning can be justified. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated premium consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home office, travel) rather than a broad consumer expansion. The evidence shows growing premiumisation among home consumers and Franke’s existing professional machines are already trusted by prosumers, so a premium positioning can be justified. Target customer: Home consumers who value professional-grade coffee quality and are willing to pay a premium for consistent brews, particularly in specific use cases such as home offices, travel, and small retail.. Value proposition: A professional-grade coffee machine that delivers consistent, high-quality brews using Swiss engineering, positioned as a premium lifestyle product for consumers who prioritize taste and reliability.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs. Standard Messaging Test (300 participants, 6 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness to pay at a premium price. If the premium purchase rate is at least 30%, proceed to develop the differentiated premium product;. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay a premium price and the size of the target segment are uncertain. The test will resolve this, but market demand remains unproven.. Would change if: If the test shows the premium purchase rate below 20%, indicating limited consumer demand, the recommendation would shift to focus on the existing professional line and avoid a differentiated consumer product.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a premium product in a specific use case, the recommendation could be updated to prioritize that segment.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and preparedness product for families, because they view CPR as a life-saving skill they should be able to perform in emergencies. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.. Why behaviour changes: Increased public awareness of home cardiac arrests and the success of bystander CPR in public cases creates a perceived need for home preparedness.. How value is captured: Laerdal can sell premium-priced home CPR kits directly to consumers, generate recurring revenue through optional training modules or subscription services, and build brand trust through family-focused messaging.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that can save lives.; Marketing can effectively communicate the safety and preparedness benefits to homeowners.; Distribution channels (e.g., online, retail) can reach target consumers.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners will show higher intent to purchase a home CPR kit if framed as a family preparedness product.; Sales of a consumer-facing home CPR kit will be positively correlated with public awareness campaigns about bystander CPR.; Consumers will be more likely to recommend the product to others if it is positioned as a safety tool for families..

T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is integrated into existing consumer health devices (e.g., smartwatches, fitness trackers) as a complementary wellness feature, because they already engage with health technology and seek convenience. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who already own or would purchase smart health devices.. Why behaviour changes: The convenience of learning CPR while monitoring health metrics and the perceived integration of wellness features make the product more attractive than a standalone kit.. How value is captured: Laerdal can license its CPR technology to consumer electronics manufacturers, earn royalties, and sell bundled kits through existing channels, leveraging the existing consumer health ecosystem.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a CPR feature integrated into their existing health devices.; Manufacturers will partner with Laerdal to embed CPR functionality in consumer products.; The integration will not significantly increase the cost of the consumer product.. Predictions: A survey of smartwatch owners will show higher intent to purchase a CPR-integrated kit compared to a standalone kit.; Sales of a consumer-facing CPR kit will be positively correlated with the presence of health-tracking features in the device.; Consumers will be more likely to recommend the product if it is marketed as a wellness add-on..

Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Home CPR Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging conditions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 homeowners (ages 25-55) recruited via a panel, stratified by home ownership and health-tracking device ownership.. Measure: 1) Intent to purchase a home CPR kit (binary: "Would you buy this kit?"). 2) WTP (EUR) for the kit. 3) Preference for messaging: "family preparedness" vs. "health wellness add-on" vs. "no purchase".. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the "family preparedness" messaging condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the "health wellness add-on" messaging condition.. Decision rule: If the "family preparedness" condition achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and WTP ≥ €30, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners. If the "health wellness add-on" condition achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% and WTP ≥ €30, develop a consumer proposition integrated with smart health devices. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on family preparedness messaging. Conduct a low-cost test (e.g., a willingness-to-pay survey with randomized messaging) to validate demand before full-scale development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or the mechanisms by which homeowners would purchase a home CPR kit. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on family preparedness messaging. Conduct a low-cost willingness-to-pay survey with randomized messaging to validate demand before full-scale development. Target customer: Homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.. Value proposition: A premium-priced home CPR kit marketed as a safety and preparedness product for families, offering flexible learning and optional training modules to build brand trust and recurring revenue.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €15,000 willingness-to-pay survey with 500 homeowners, comparing "family preparedness" messaging against "health wellness add-on" messaging, and use the decision rule to decide on product development.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay and purchase intent for a home CPR kit are unknown; the test may not capture real consumer behavior. The competitive landscape and existing consumer health devices also introduce uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent below 30% or willingness to pay below €30 for the "family preparedness" messaging, the investment would be reconsidered in favor of no expansion.; If independent data shows strong consumer demand for home CPR kits, the recommendation would shift toward a consumer proposition.; If a competitor launches a successful consumer home CPR product, the market opportunity would be reassessed.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Convenience vs Sustainability" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase scenario.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners and small business owners (recruited via panel) who have purchased floor-cleaning equipment in the past 12 months.. Measure: 1) Choice of product variant (compact version of CS5 Micro-Scrubber vs standard version). 2) Willingness to pay premium (price difference between variants). 3) Statement of importance (convenience vs sustainability).. Predictions: T1: At least 15% more homeowners will select the compact version when convenience is emphasized, and willingness to pay premium will be higher for the compact version.; T2: At least 15% more environmentally conscious respondents will select the compact version when sustainability is emphasized, and willingness to pay premium will be higher for the compact version.. Decision rule: If the compact version's choice rate exceeds the standard version's rate by ≥15 percentage points and the premium price difference exceeds €20, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Cost-Saving vs Trust-Based Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision.. Sample: 400 homeowners in Germany and the UK, recruited via panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership.. Measure: 1) Choice: which product (Testo portable device) they would purchase (Yes/No). 2) Willingness to pay (WTP): maximum price they would pay for each product. 3) Messaging effect: whether a cost-saving message (T1) or a trusted recommendation message (T2) increases purchase intent.. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will choose the cost-saving version when presented with a 10% heating cost reduction claim.; T2: At least 30% will choose the trusted recommendation version when presented with a "recommended by local authority" label.. Decision rule: If the proportion of respondents choosing the cost-saving version exceeds 30% and the difference is statistically significant (p<0.05), we conclude T1 is supported. If the trusted recommendation version exceeds 30% and the difference is significant, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither exceeds 30% or the difference is not significant, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes cost-saving benefits for homeowners, supported by evidence of market demand and willingness to pay for energy‑efficiency tools. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address homeowner motivations, trust, or purchase decisions for Testo instruments. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: Homeowners will adopt Testo portable measuring instruments for home energy efficiency if they view the devices as a tool for reducing heating costs and improving home comfort.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes cost-saving benefits for homeowners, supported by evidence of market demand and willingness to pay for energy‑efficiency tools. Target customer: Homeowners in Germany and the UK who are interested in reducing heating costs and improving home comfort.. Value proposition: A Testo portable measuring instrument marketed as a cost‑saving DIY energy audit tool, offering clear return‑on‑investment messaging and optional subscription services for real‑time energy data analysis.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Test (choice‑based conjoint survey) to measure purchase intent under cost‑saving vs trusted recommendation messaging.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the exact willingness to pay for a Testo device remain uncertain; the decline in the Consumer segment (22% revenue drop) suggests limited current consumer demand.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the trusted recommendation version exceeds 30% and the difference is statistically significant, we would reconsider the strategy and explore trust‑based messaging.; If the test shows neither messaging version exceeds 30% or the difference is not significant, we would conclude neither theory is strongly supported and would recommend further market research.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Method: Online survey with two arms: (1) DIY arm presents a simplified, low-cost DIY insulation kit with clear instructions and materials; (2) Professional arm presents a professional installation service with a safety-compliance guarantee. T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer CPR home training product because they view it as a private, convenient way to learn a life-saving skill, and they trust the brand and regulatory endorsement. Who benefits: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies; Laerdal benefits from premium pricing and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional/medical task to a personal, routine health skill when it is delivered in a private, home environment and accompanied by clear, regulated guidance.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells a branded, regulated home kit at a premium price, and can license the brand to other consumer health devices.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the brand and regulatory endorsement more than generic home CPR resources.; Home CPR training is perceived as a private, discreet activity suitable for households.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a branded, regulated product.. Predictions: In a test offering a branded home CPR kit, purchase intent among households will be higher than for an identical unbranded kit.; Consumers will report higher confidence in performing CPR correctly when the kit bears a recognized brand and carries regulatory certification..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer CPR home training product because they need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies, and they trust the brand and regulatory endorsement as a signal of safety. Who benefits: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies; Laerdal benefits from brand extension and premium pricing.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional/medical task to a personal, routine health skill when they perceive the product as regulated, trusted, and backed by a reputable brand.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells a branded, regulated home kit at a premium price, and can license the brand to other consumer health devices.. Assumptions: Consumers associate brand and regulatory endorsement with safety and efficacy.; Home CPR training is perceived as a necessary, life-saving skill rather than a luxury.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that is trusted by health authorities.. Predictions: In a test offering a branded home CPR kit, purchase intent among households will be higher than for an identical unbranded kit.; Consumers will report higher confidence in performing CPR correctly when the kit bears a recognized brand and carries regulatory certification..

Test "Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled online survey with a choice between a branded home CPR kit (Laerdal brand, regulatory certification) and an identical unbranded home CPR kit. Participants are recruited from households in the United States with at least one adult member. Each participant sees one of the two kits and is asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the maximum price they would pay.. Sample: Proposed sample: 500 households (1,000 participants) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect the U.S. population.. Measure: Primary measure: average purchase intent score for the branded kit versus the unbranded kit. Secondary measure: maximum price participants would pay for the branded kit.. Predictions: T1: Branded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the unbranded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).; T2: Unbranded kit will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than the branded kit, and the difference will be statistically significant (p < 0.05).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the branded kit is at least 1.5 points higher than the unbranded kit and the difference is statistically significant, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training). If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Laerdal already offers a branded home CPR program (CPR Anytime) and that consumers are prepared to perform CPR in homes, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will purchase a branded home kit at a premium price. A controlled test is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows Laerdal already offers a branded home CPR program (CPR Anytime) and that consumers are prepared to perform CPR in homes, but it does not demonstrate that consumers will purchase a branded home kit at a premium price. A controlled test is needed to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity. Target customer: Individuals and families who need to be prepared for cardiac emergencies, particularly those who currently lack access to professional training.. Value proposition: A branded, regulated home CPR kit that delivers private, convenient training and can be shared with family members, leveraging Laerdal’s reputation and regulatory endorsement to justify a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Branded vs Unbranded Home CPR Kit Purchase Test (500 households, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and price sensitivity before committing to a consumer product.. Uncertainty: Whether consumers will actually purchase the branded kit at a premium price, and whether the perceived value of brand and regulation outweighs price sensitivity.. Would change if: If the test shows the branded kit achieving a purchase intent difference of at least 1.5 points and a statistically significant p-value, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition.; If the test shows the unbranded kit achieving higher purchase intent or that price sensitivity is high, we would reconsider the investment.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Current reach to individual buyers is unknown; must be discovered.; Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive advantage.; Investment must be evaluated against the existing professional product line and Franke’s overall business model.. T1: Home consumers will purchase Franke coffee machines if they perceive them as premium, professional-grade equipment that offers superior taste and convenience, because they are willing to pay a premium for quality and brand prestige. Who benefits: Franke Coffee Systems captures value through premium pricing and higher margins on differentiated consumer offerings.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from generic household appliances to professional-grade machines when they associate the machine with higher quality, brand reputation, and a perception of professional expertise, leading them to choose a differentiated Fran. How value is captured: By selling a differentiated consumer line at premium prices and leveraging Franke’s professional brand reputation, Franke can achieve higher revenue per unit and maintain its premium positioning.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality and brand prestige.; Franke’s professional reputation translates into consumer trust.; The market size for premium home coffee machines is sufficient to justify investment.. Predictions: A survey of target consumers will show a willingness to pay at least 20% more for a Franke machine compared to a comparable generic machine.; Sales of the differentiated consumer line will exceed sales of the existing professional line in the same segment within the first year.; Brand perception studies will indicate that consumers associate Franke with professional coffee expertise..

T2: Home consumers will purchase Franke coffee machines if they perceive them as a convenient, integrated solution that simplifies coffee preparation, because they value time savings and ease of use. Who benefits: Franke Coffee Systems captures value through higher unit volume sales and reduced customer support costs from a simplified product offering.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers adopt a differentiated Franke machine when it offers a streamlined experience that reduces the time and effort required to prepare coffee, making it more attractive than traditional or generic machines.. How value is captured: By positioning the machine as a time-saving, integrated solution and pricing it accordingly, Franke can achieve higher average revenue per unit and scale sales across multiple consumer segments.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience and time savings in coffee machine selection.; The integrated design of Franke machines provides a clear advantage over competitors.; The market size for convenience-focused home coffee machines is sufficient to justify investment.. Predictions: A survey of target consumers will show a willingness to pay at least 15% more for a Franke machine compared to a comparable convenience-focused machine.; Sales of the differentiated consumer line will exceed sales of the existing professional line in the same segment within the first year.; Consumer reviews will emphasize time savings and ease of use as primary purchase drivers..

Test "Premium vs Convenience Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view a product description of a Franke consumer machine (identical spec) and are asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) at three price points: 1) current professional price, 2) 20% premium over professional price, 3) 15% premium over a convenience-focused competitor (e.g., a machine with integrated grinder and pre-ground bean option). They also rate importance of taste/quality (high) vs convenience (high) on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 UK adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income to reflect the target consumer segment.. Measure: Average WTP at each price point and the proportion of respondents choosing the premium price versus the convenience competitor.. Predictions: T1: Participants will show higher average WTP at the 20% premium price and a higher proportion will choose the premium price than at the convenience competitor.; T2: Participants will show higher average WTP at the convenience competitor price and a higher proportion will choose the convenience competitor than at the premium price.. Decision rule: If the premium price WTP average is at least 15% higher than the convenience competitor price WTP average, proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If the premium price WTP average is at least 15% lower than the convenience competitor price WTP average, develop a convenience-focused proposition. If the premium price WTP average is between 5% and 15% lower than the convenience competitor price WTP average, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated premium consumer proposition targeting home consumers who value professional-grade coffee quality and brand prestige. The evidence shows growing premiumisation among home consumers and Franke’s existing professional positioning, but the test is needed to confirm willingness to pay and competitive positioning. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result concerns a warehouse label printer and does not address consumer purchasing behavior, taste perception, or convenience. Therefore it provides no evidence for or against T1, which predicts premium-driven consumer demand. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated premium consumer proposition targeting home consumers who value professional-grade coffee quality and brand prestige. The evidence shows growing premiumisation among home consumers and Franke’s existing professional positioning, but the proposed test is needed to confirm willingness to pay and competitive positioning. Target customer: Home consumers in the UK and adjacent markets who purchase coffee machines for personal use and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality and brand prestige.. Value proposition: A Franke consumer machine positioned as a premium, professional-grade coffee solution that delivers superior taste and convenience through integrated design and adjustable grinding, sold at a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs Convenience Messaging Test (300 UK adults, 6 weeks, €18,000) to measure willingness to pay at three price points and compare against a convenience-focused competitor. Use the decision rule to decide whether to. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a premium consumer proposition is unknown; the test is needed to quantify it. Additionally, the size of the premium market and Franke’s ability to capture value at premium prices remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the premium price WTP average is at least 15% lower than the convenience competitor price WTP average, we would shift focus to a convenience-focused proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference in WTP between the premium and convenience price points, we would recommend further market research before committing to either proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

How value is captured: Premium pricing, limited edition designs, subscription services for maintenance, and direct-to-consumer sales channels increase margins.. T2: Home consumers are price-sensitive and prefer cost-effective solutions, leading them to avoid premium-priced machines and seek affordable alternatives, limiting demand for differentiated consumer propositions. Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Lifestyle vs. Value Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home coffee drinkers (n=500). They view a product description of a Franke coffee machine with identical technical specifications but presented in two versions: (A) Lifestyle version emphasizing design, brand, and lifestyle benefits; (B) Value version emphasizing price, cost savings, and essential functionality. After viewing, participants indicate (1) willingness to pay a premium (binary: ≥ 20% above base price) and (2) purchase intent (binary: would buy).. Sample: 500 home coffee drinkers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and coffee frequency.. Measure: Willingness to pay premium (binary) and purchase intent (binary).. Predictions: T1: Lifestyle version will generate higher willingness to pay premium and purchase intent than value version.; T2: Value version will generate higher willingness to pay premium and purchase intent than lifestyle version.. Decision rule: If willingness to pay premium for lifestyle version exceeds value version by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 45% vs 35%), proceed to develop a differentiated lifestyle proposition. If value version exceeds by 10 points, recommend a value-focused expansion. If neither exceeds by 10 points, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home consumers who value lifestyle and design, rather than expanding the existing professional line or focusing solely on volume sales. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Performance Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view a product description of a new floor scrubber (T360) and are asked to indicate (a) likelihood to purchase at a premium price, (b) willingness to purchase multiple units for different spaces, (c) importance of design status, and (d) importance of performance benefits (e.g., faster cleaning, lower water usage). After viewing, they are asked to rank the product on a 1‑10 scale (1‑very unlikely, 10‑very likely)..
