Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Outdoor vs Health Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase intent and willingness to pay. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Outdoor (protective gloves marketed as outdoor recreation lifestyle accessory) or Health (protective gloves marketed as health and hygiene necessity). Both conditions present the same glove product with identical features but different messaging.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 outdoor enthusiasts (recruited via outdoor recreation forums) and 250 health-conscious consumers (recruited via health and wellness platforms). Stratify by age and gender to ensure diversity.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness to pay (EUR) for the product in each condition. Secondary measure: purchase intent (percentage of participants indicating "Would buy at price X" where X is a premium price).. Predictions: T1: Outdoor condition will show higher average willingness to pay and purchase intent than Health condition.; T2: Health condition will show higher average willingness to pay and purchase intent than Outdoor condition.. Decision rule: If the average willingness to pay in the Outdoor condition exceeds the Health condition by at least 10% (i.e., Outdoor ≥ Health +10%) and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), then T1 is supported and a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation is recommended. If the difference is ≤ 10% or not statistically significant, then T2 is supported and a differentiated consumer proposition targeting health necessity is recommended. If neither condition meets the threshold, the investment is not justified.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Family vs Personal Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants are recruited from a panel of adults (n=400). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a personal health message emphasizing the consumer benefits of learning CPR for family emergencies (e.g., 'Protect your family by learning CPR at home'). Condition B receives a family-friendly message emphasizing shared learning and bonding (e.g., 'Teach your family CPR together and create quality family time'). Both conditions present the same product (Laerdal CPR Anytime home training kit). Participants are asked to report purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 400 adults aged 18-65, screened for interest in home CPR training.. Measure: Purchase intent (1-7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Condition A.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Condition A and Condition B is >= 1.5 points, we conclude that personal health messaging (T1) is more effective. If the difference is <= 1.5 points, we conclude that family-friendly messaging (T2) is more effective. If both conditions show similar intent, we recommend further testing.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CPR training for individuals) that emphasizes personal health responsibility and family protection. Begin with a low-cost online survey test to validate purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Individual consumers aged 18-65 who want to learn CPR for family emergencies.. Value proposition: A portable, easy-to-share home CPR kit that empowers consumers to protect their families, offering a premium price point and optional subscription for updates and certification.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 1.5 points relative to a control condition, we would reconsider the investment.; If a separate test shows strong demand for family-friendly messaging, we would shift focus to a family-oriented proposition.; If willingness to pay is significantly lower than €50-€100, we would explore lower-priced or subscription models.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a personal health responsibility and delivered through a trusted brand, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay. Who benefits: Individual consumers who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies and feel a personal responsibility to act.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR as a professional task to a personal duty when they see it framed as a health responsibility and when they trust the brand associated with professional medical expertise.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium pricing for consumer kits, subscription models for ongoing training, and direct-to-consumer sales that leverage its brand credibility.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to invest in personal health preparedness.; The brand association with Laerdal's professional medical reputation transfers to consumer perception.; A differentiated consumer proposition can be developed within budget and time constraints.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused CPR kit, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic health product.; Willingness to pay will be above the price point of a standard health product.; Customers will report higher perceived trust in the brand compared to competitors..

T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is integrated into existing consumer health routines and recommended by trusted health professionals, leading to higher adoption rates and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Health-conscious consumers who already engage in daily health activities and trust professional medical recommendations.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers adopt new health products when they see them as part of a familiar routine and when they receive endorsement from trusted professionals, reducing perceived risk and increasing perceived benefit.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through bundled consumer health products, subscription services for routine check-ins, and partnerships with healthcare providers to recommend the kit.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to integrate new health products into their daily routines.; Health professionals' recommendations significantly influence consumer purchase decisions.; A differentiated consumer proposition can be positioned as a complement to existing health habits.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-focused CPR kit bundled with a daily health routine product, adoption rates will be higher than for a standalone CPR kit.; Consumers will report higher intent to purchase when the kit is recommended by a healthcare professional.; Repeat purchase rates will be higher for consumers who received a recommendation versus those who chose the product independently..

Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the personal responsibility version is at least 10 points higher than for the professional recommendation version, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on personal responsibility. The pilot will provide the necessary data to resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the personal responsibility version is at least 10 points higher than for the professional recommendation version, we would proceed with a consumer proposition focused on personal responsibility.; If the pilot shows no significant difference in purchase intent between the two exposure versions, we would reconsider the investment and explore alternative strategies such as a hybrid model or no expansion.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home kitchen dishwashers) with dedicated branding, marketing, and sales channels.; 2) Expand the existing commercial product line into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., add a consumer‑grade glasswasher).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on commercial dishwashers and glasswashers, possibly deepening existing B2B relationships.; 4) Change the route to buyers: partner with retailers or online platforms to reach consumers directly, leveraging existing distribution networks.; 5) Target a different customer group: shift focus to small restaurants, cafes, or hotel chains rather than large commercial facilities..

T1: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated Winterhalter consumer dishwasher if they perceive it as a premium, high-quality, space-saving solution that integrates seamlessly into their kitchen, because they value convenience, hygiene, and modern design. Who benefits: Individual homeowners in small to medium households who currently lack a dishwasher or prefer a compact, undercounter unit.. Why behaviour changes: Growing consumer awareness of hygiene and convenience, combined with the availability of compact models, makes a premium undercounter dishwasher attractive for home use.. How value is captured: Winterhalter can charge a premium price for a differentiated consumer model, sell through specialty retailers or online channels, and capture recurring service and replacement revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a premium, high-quality undercounter dishwasher.; Winterhalter can adapt its existing UC Series to meet home-use requirements without significant redesign.; Retail distribution channels are available for a differentiated consumer product.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show a willingness to pay at least 20% more for a Winterhalter undercounter dishwasher compared to a standard model.; Sales of a differentiated consumer model would be higher in regions where undercounter dishwashers are already popular.; Customers would report higher satisfaction with the product due to its compact size and integrated design..

T2: Homeowners will adopt a differentiated Winterhalter consumer dishwasher if they perceive it as a sustainable, eco-friendly product that reduces water and energy consumption, because they are increasingly concerned about environmental impact. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious homeowners who prioritize sustainable appliances.. Why behaviour changes: Growing consumer awareness of water and energy efficiency, combined with the availability of eco-certified products, makes a sustainable undercounter dishwasher attractive for home use.. How value is captured: Winterhalter can market the product as eco-friendly, potentially command a premium price, and capture recurring revenue through service and replacement of sustainable components.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for an eco-certified dishwasher.; Winterhalter can modify existing models to meet sustainability standards without significant redesign.; Environmental messaging can effectively reach target homeowners.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show a willingness to pay at least 15% more for an eco-certified Winterhalter undercounter dishwasher compared to a standard model.; Sales of an eco-differentiated model would be higher in regions where environmental concerns are prominent.; Customers would report higher satisfaction with the product due to its sustainability credentials..

Does not show: It does not show that homeowners actually desire a differentiated consumer model or that they would pay a premium for it..

Test "Premium vs Eco-Differentiated Winterhalter Undercounter Dishwasher Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income, with a secondary group of 100 small restaurant owners.. Measure: 1) Average WTP (in euros) for a differentiated undercounter dishwasher described as premium (high-quality, space-saving) versus eco (sustainability-focused). 2) Intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2) and stated primary purchase driver (premium, eco, or other).. Predictions: T1: Premium segment will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than eco segment, and the majority will cite premium as the primary driver.; T2: Eco segment will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than premium segment, and the majority will cite eco as the primary driver.. Decision rule: If premium WTP ≥ €1,200 AND premium purchase intent ≥ 55% AND premium is cited by ≥ 60% of respondents, proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition. If eco WTP ≥ €1,200 AND eco purchase intent ≥ 55% AND eco is cited by ≥ 60% of respondents, develop an eco‑differentiated proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Winterhalter already offers a configurable undercounter dishwasher (UC Series) that can be adapted for home use, and there is no public evidence of strong consumer demand for a premium differentiated model. The proposed test (Premium vs Eco-Differentiated Winterhalter Undercounter Dishwasher Test) is the next step to validate the Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivations for premium or eco differentiated dishwashers. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The proposed test is the next step to validate the Target customer: Individual homeowners in small to medium households who currently lack a dishwasher or prefer a compact, undercounter unit.. Value proposition: A premium, high-quality undercounter dishwasher that integrates seamlessly into the kitchen, offering convenience, hygiene, and modern design, sold through specialty retailers or online channels.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Premium vs Eco-Differentiated Winterhalter Undercounter Dishwasher Test (300 homeowners, €18,000, 8 weeks) to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for a premium versus eco-differentiated model.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market and the willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for a differentiated model are unknown. The test will clarify whether demand exists and at what price point.. Would change if: If the test shows premium WTP ≥ €1,200, purchase intent ≥ 55%, and premium is cited by ≥ 60% of respondents, we would proceed to develop a differentiated premium consumer proposition.; If the test shows eco WTP ≥ €1,200, purchase intent ≥ 55%, and eco is cited by ≥ 60% of respondents, we would develop an eco-differentiated proposition.; If neither premium nor eco segment meets the thresholds, we would recommend no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a precision tool for accurate ingredient measurement, because they value repeatable results for cooking and food preparation. Who benefits: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer scales lack precision; a scale that measures by weight reliably reduces guesswork and improves recipe accuracy.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can charge a premium for precision features and sell through direct channels, leveraging its brand reputation for accuracy.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for precision over basic features.; Marketing can effectively communicate the precision benefit to home users.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a precision digital scale to home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard digital scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a standard scale by at least 20%..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated digital kitchen scale if it is marketed as a health and wellness tool for portion control and carbohydrate counting, because they seek tools that support dietary goals. Who benefits: Individuals following specific diets (e.g., low-carb, keto) and health-conscious consumers.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers already use digital scales for weight monitoring and want a tool that directly supports their dietary objectives.. How value is captured: Mettler-Toledo can position the scale as a health companion, justify a premium price, and sell through direct channels or specialty retailers.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for features that directly support their diet.; Marketing can effectively link the scale to health and wellness messaging.; Direct sales can reach individual buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a health-focused digital scale, purchase intent will be higher than for a precision-focused scale.; Willingness to pay will be above the price of a precision scale by at least 15%..

T2 supports, from mettler-nhs-carb-counting (independent_study): "Weighing foods give you a more accurate measure to work out the carbohydrate content. …". Does not show: It does not show consumer willingness to pay a premium for health-focused features or that they would purchase a differentiated scale..

T2 neutral, from mettler-atk-by-weight (independent_study): "Measuring ingredients by weight is the only way to ensure predictable results.". Does not show: It does not address consumer motivation for health-focused features or willingness to pay for them..

Test "Precision vs Health Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants see one of two product descriptions of a digital kitchen scale: Precision version emphasizing accurate gram measurement for reliable recipe results; Health version emphasizing portion control and carbohydrate counting for dietary goals. They are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 300 U.S. adults, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and dietary interest (approx. 150 per condition).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay.. Predictions: T1: Precision version will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Health version.; T2: Health version will achieve higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Precision version.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Precision version exceeds Health version by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed with a precision-focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, proceed with a health-focused proposition. If both conditions are met, proceed with a dual proposition.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a precision-focused consumer proposition for home cooks, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s existing brand reputation for accuracy and direct sales channels. Conduct a low‑cost test to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for precision features before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a precision-focused consumer proposition for home cooks, leveraging Mettler-Toledo’s existing brand reputation for accuracy and direct sales channels. Conduct a low‑cost test to validate consumer willingness to pay a premium for precision features before scaling. Target customer: Home cooks and food preparers who need reliable weight measurement for recipes and portion control.. Value proposition: A precision digital kitchen scale that measures by weight with accurate gram resolution, ensuring predictable recipe results and reducing guesswork.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Precision vs Health Messaging Test (300 U.S. adults, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for precision versus health messaging.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for precision features is uncertain; the test will determine whether demand justifies investment.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the precision version is at least 1.5 points higher than for the health version, we would proceed with a precision-focused proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or lower willingness to pay, we would reconsider expansion or explore other alternatives.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential smart HVAC products if they perceive them as a premium, energy‑saving upgrade that offers precise temperature control and integration with existing smart home ecosystems. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking comfort and energy savings; Belimo gains premium pricing and brand differentiation.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of energy costs and smart home convenience motivates homeowners to replace traditional thermostats with smart, programmable devices.. How value is captured: Belimo can charge a premium price for its integrated smart actuators and valves, leveraging its existing OEM relationships to reach consumers through retail or direct channels.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for energy‑efficient, smart HVAC solutions.; Belimo can scale production and distribution to meet consumer demand without compromising B2B relationships.; Smart home integration capabilities are technically feasible and accepted by homeowners.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 30% indicating intent to purchase a Belimo smart thermostat within the next 12 months.; Sales of Belimo residential smart actuators would increase in regions with higher energy‑cost awareness.; Competitor smart thermostat offerings would not significantly erode Belimo's market share in the residential segment..

T2: Homeowners will adopt Belimo residential smart HVAC products if they perceive them as a cost‑saving, long‑term investment that reduces energy bills and maintenance needs, rather than as a premium lifestyle upgrade. Who benefits: Homeowners focused on long‑term cost savings and lower maintenance; Belimo gains recurring revenue and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Economic uncertainty and rising energy costs make homeowners seek solutions that directly lower monthly expenses and reduce future repair costs.. How value is captured: Belimo can offer subscription services for performance monitoring and maintenance alerts, and sell durable, high‑efficiency actuators at competitive prices, capturing value through recurring revenue and volume sales.. Assumptions: Homeowners prioritize long‑term cost savings over immediate premium features.; Belimo can provide clear evidence of energy savings and reduced maintenance costs.; Subscription services for performance monitoring are acceptable to consumers.. Predictions: A survey of homeowners would show at least 40% indicating intent to purchase a Belimo smart thermostat if it promises annual energy savings of at least €200.; Sales of Belimo residential smart actuators would be higher in regions with higher average energy bills.; Customers would be more likely to recommend Belimo if they cite cost savings as a primary reason..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Residential Smart HVAC Actuators" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two distinct scenarios presented to homeowners. Scenario A presents a Belimo smart thermostat with a premium price (e.g., €300) and emphasizes energy savings and smart home integration. Scenario B presents the same product at a lower price (e.g., €150) and emphasizes long-term cost savings and reduced maintenance. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each scenario.. Sample: 400 U.S. homeowners who have central air conditioning and own a programmable thermostat, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by household income to reflect diverse economic profiles.. Measure: Maximum price participants would pay for Scenario A (premium version) and Scenario B (cost-saving version).. Predictions: T1: Participants will indicate a higher maximum price for Scenario A than for Scenario B, indicating willingness to pay a premium for energy savings and smart home integration.; T2: Participants will indicate a higher maximum price for Scenario B than for Scenario A, indicating willingness to pay a lower price for long-term cost savings.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price for Scenario A exceeds Scenario B by at least €50, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing premium features (T1). If Scenario B exceeds Scenario A by at least €50, pursue a cost‑saving proposition (T2). If the difference is less than €50, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home energy management and smart home integration) by offering a premium Belimo smart thermostat at a price point that reflects its integrated capabilities. Use the proposed willingness-to-pay survey to validate consumer demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Sample: 300 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across Brand Trust and Regulatory Compliance conditions.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and stated brand trust in the Brand Trust Condition than in the Regulatory Compliance Condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and stated regulatory compliance in the Regulatory Compliance Condition than in the Brand Trust Condition.. Test "Home CPR Kit Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product concepts: (1) premium-priced home CPR kit (e.g., Laerdal Anytime) marketed as a private, convenient solution for family training; (2) low-cost, bulk B2B training kit marketed as a professional solution. Participants indicate whether they would purchase each kit and cite reasons (privacy/convenience vs cost/need).. Sample: 400 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect U.S. households. Randomly assigned to see either the premium-priced kit or the low-cost kit.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason (open-ended) for choosing each kit.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent for the premium-priced kit and higher frequency of citing privacy/convenience as the primary reason.; T2: Higher purchase intent for the low-cost kit and higher frequency of citing cost/need as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the premium-priced kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and privacy/convenience reasons ≥ 30% of respondents, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training. If the low-cost kit achieves purchase intent ≥ 40% and cost/need reasons ≥ 30%, consider a low‑cost consumer offering. If neither meets threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Safety Necessity vs Lifestyle Accessory" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from homeowners who have not purchased a home safety device in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (A) Safety necessity messaging emphasizing reliability, affordability, and professional-grade medical safety; (B) Lifestyle accessory messaging emphasizing design, personal style, and integration into home aesthetics. Both conditions present the same Dräger consumer product (e.g., CO detector). Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 homeowners (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home ownership status.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay in the safety necessity condition compared to the lifestyle condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay in the lifestyle condition compared to the safety necessity condition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in the safety necessity condition is at least 5 points higher than in the lifestyle condition (i.e., average intent ≥ 5.5), proceed to develop a safety‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 points, the lifestyle proposition is more likely to succeed and the investment is justified. If the difference is ≤ 5 points, both propositions are unlikely to succeed and no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a safety‑focused consumer proposition for homeowners, targeting CO and gas detectors. The evidence shows a demonstrated need for home safety awareness and Dräger’s existing consumer product availability, making a safety‑focused approach the most evidence‑driven option. The lifestyle proposition remains uncertain due to limited evidence of consumer willingness to pay for design‑focused safety devices.. Would change if: If the test shows a ≥ 5‑point difference in purchase intent between safety necessity and lifestyle messaging, we would prioritize the safety proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a lifestyle‑focused safety device at a premium price, we would reconsider the lifestyle approach.; If Dräger’s existing consumer product (e.g., Alcotest 4000) demonstrates strong sales or brand recognition, we would reassess the need for a new differentiated proposition.. Test "Home Gas Detector Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online controlled experiment with two between‑subjects conditions. Participants view a product description of a compliant home CO detector (T1) or a design‑focused home gas detector (T2). Both versions are priced at a premium comparable to non‑compliant alternatives. Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not likely to 7‑very likely) and state the primary reason for purchase.. Sample: 400 adults (200 per condition) recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution of target consumers (homeowners, renters, age 25‑55).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of safety concern for the compliant version than for the design version.; T2: Higher purchase intent and primary reason of design/brand appeal for the design version than for the compliant version.. Decision rule: If the design version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the compliant version and at least 20 percentage points above the baseline (1), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the compliant version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher and the design version is not significantly better, focus on safety‑driven B2B expansion. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance and awareness, rather than a lifestyle or fashion proposition. Begin with a low‑cost test of purchase intent for a compliant CO detector to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home CO detector) that emphasizes safety compliance and awareness, rather than a lifestyle or fashion proposition. Begin with a low‑cost test of purchase intent for a compliant CO detector to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners and renters who face CO risks from cooking, heating, or ventilation.. Value proposition: A trusted, compliant home gas detector that raises awareness of CO poisoning risks and provides peace of mind, leveraging Dräger’s safety brand credibility to justify a premium price.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed 10‑week, €18,000 online purchase‑intent test with 400 adults, comparing a compliant CO detector to a design‑focused alternative. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with development.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for home gas detectors and the willingness to pay a premium for compliance are uncertain. Regulatory feasibility for consumer products is also unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows the design version’s purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than the compliant version and at least 20 percentage points above the baseline, we would shift focus to a lifestyle proposition.; If the test fails to meet the thresholds or shows no significant difference, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on B2B markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Premium vs Cost-Saving Messaging Test for Residential Smart Actuators" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from regions with varying energy cost awareness. Participants see one of two product descriptions for a Belimo residential smart actuator: (A) Premium messaging emphasizing energy savings, precise temperature control, and smart home integration; (B) Cost-saving messaging emphasizing annual energy bill savings, reduced maintenance needs, and long-term investment. Participants then indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 homeowners in three regions: high energy cost awareness (e.g., California), moderate (e.g., Texas), and low (e.g., Florida). Recruit via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each messaging condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for premium messaging in high‑energy‑cost regions.; T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for cost‑saving messaging in high‑energy‑cost regions.. Decision rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between premium and cost‑saving messaging is ≥ 1.5 points in high‑energy‑cost regions, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, focus on cost‑saving messaging. If both regions show similar differences, the premium proposition is not justified.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., premium, energy‑saving smart HVAC actuators) targeting homeowners in high‑energy‑cost regions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Therefore it does not affect T1. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., premium, energy‑saving smart HVAC actuators) targeting homeowners in high‑energy‑cost regions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: Homeowners in high‑energy‑cost regions (e.g., California, Texas) who are aware of energy costs and seek comfort and savings.. Value proposition: Belimo's integrated smart actuators offer precise temperature control, energy savings, and seamless smart home integration, allowing homeowners to reduce monthly bills and maintenance costs while maintaining comfort.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs Cost‑Saving Messaging Test (500 homeowners in three regions) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay. Use the decision rule: if the premium messaging difference is ≥1.5 points in high‑energy‑cost areas,. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for Belimo's specific smart actuators and the competitive landscape remain uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for premium messaging below 30% in any region, the premium proposition would be reconsidered.; If a competitor offers a comparable smart actuator at a lower price, the investment case would weaken.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a description of a home CPR training kit and are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑2 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). They are then asked about their primary reason for purchase (personal preparedness, insurance/employer requirement, or other).. Sample: 400 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced across two conditions: 200 see personal preparedness messaging and 200 see compliance messaging.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑2 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: reason for purchase (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the personal preparedness condition compared to the compliance condition.; T2: Higher purchase intent and willingness to pay in the compliance condition compared to the personal preparedness condition.. Decision rule: If personal preparedness messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher than compliance messaging (e.g., mean intent 1.5 vs 1.0), recommend developing a consumer proposition focused on personal preparedness. If compliance messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher, recommend a compliance‑focused consumer proposition. If the difference is <5 points, indicate uncertainty and suggest further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, focusing on personal preparedness messaging. Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training, focusing on personal preparedness messaging. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay, and use the results to decide on pricing and distribution. Target customer: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be prepared for cardiac emergencies.. Value proposition: A home CPR training kit that empowers families to perform CPR in emergencies, leveraging Laerdal’s expertise to provide a safe, easy-to-learn solution that can save lives.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Compliance Messaging Test (400 U.S. adults, 8 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under personal preparedness vs. compliance messaging.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for a home CPR kit and the size of the consumer market remain uncertain. Evidence of strong demand is limited to market facts about home cardiac arrests, not to consumer purchase behavior.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 20% or willingness to pay below €50, indicating low consumer demand, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion or a different route to market.; If compliance messaging yields purchase intent at least 10 points higher than personal preparedness messaging, the recommendation would shift toward a compliance-focused consumer proposition.. T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

Test "Messaging Test: Voluntary vs Regulatory Home Water Test Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey experiment with two randomized messaging conditions. Measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary choice: "Would you purchase this test kit?" and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: In the voluntary messaging condition, purchase intent will be at least 15 percentage points higher than in the regulatory messaging condition.; T2: In the regulatory messaging condition, purchase intent will be at least 15 percentage points higher than in the voluntary messaging condition.. Decision rule: If voluntary purchase intent exceeds regulatory purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting voluntary consumers. If regulatory purchase intent exceeds voluntary purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, pursue a compliance-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand into consumer markets.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Public evidence shows home water test kits are widely available and sold under Hach brands, but it does not demonstrate consumer demand, willingness to pay, or that consumers will act on the results. A limited messaging test (e.g., voluntary vs regulatory positioning) is needed to validate demand before committing resources. Target customer: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Hach's home water test kits as a voluntary, peace-of-mind monitoring solution, leveraging existing brand trust and distribution channels.. Public evidence does not confirm demand or that consumers will act on the results.. Would change if: If the messaging test shows voluntary purchase intent exceeding regulatory purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, we would proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting voluntary consumers.; If the test shows regulatory purchase intent exceeding voluntary purchase intent by at least 15 percentage points in both regions, we would pursue a compliance-focused proposition.; If neither condition is met, we would maintain the current B2B focus and not expand into consumer markets.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: unlikely.

T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

Test "Consumer Intent Test: Willingness to Pay for Home Water Test Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question. Participants are recruited from a panel matching the demographic distribution of homeowners in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are shown a product description of a home water test kit and asked: "How much would you pay for a single test kit?" They also indicate whether they would purchase it if it were required by a local regulation (T2) or if they already own a test kit (T1).. Sample: 500 participants (150 from regions with strict water quality laws and 150 from regions with moderate laws), balanced for age, gender, and income.. Measure: Average WTP for a single test kit (EUR) and binary purchase intent (required by regulation vs. already own kit).. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in regions with strict water quality laws compared to moderate laws.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for a single test kit in the strict-law group exceeds the average WTP in the moderate-law group by at least €10, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting that segment. If the difference is less than €10, the evidence is insufficient to justify investment and no further action is recommended.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

T2: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they need to comply with local water quality regulations or safety standards, making DIY testing a legal requirement rather than a voluntary choice. Who benefits: Homeowners and renters in regions with strict water quality laws who must test their water to ensure compliance.. Why behaviour changes: Regulatory pressure and the need to avoid fines or legal action create a mandatory need for accurate water testing, shifting behavior from voluntary to required.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through compliance-focused sales of test kits, accessories, and potentially subscription services for regulatory reporting.. Assumptions: Regulatory bodies enforce water quality testing in target regions; Consumers are aware of and comply with these regulations; Hach's products meet the required standards for regulatory compliance. Predictions: Sales of compliance-focused test kits will increase in regions with strict water quality laws; Consumers will purchase kits at higher volumes when marketed as required by regulation; Regulatory bodies will report increased adoption of DIY testing kits in compliance regions.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Water Test Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a sample of homeowners and renters in regions with varying water quality regulations. Participants are offered a mock premium test kit at two price points: $20 (one-time test) and $40 (reusable strips and accessories). They are asked: (1) How likely are they to purchase the kit? (2) What would be the maximum price they would pay for a reusable version? (3) Why would they choose to purchase? (open-ended).. Sample: 500 respondents (200 in regions with strict water quality laws, 200 in regions with moderate laws, 100 in regions with few regulations). Recruit via online panels to match demographic distribution.. Measure: Share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at each price point, plus average maximum price willingness to pay for a reusable version.. Predictions: T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent at the $40 price point than at $20, especially in regions with strict regulations.; T2: Purchase intent and willingness to pay are similar across price points and do not differ by regulatory region.. Decision rule: If the share of respondents indicating "high" likelihood to purchase at $40 exceeds 30% and exceeds the share at $20 by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on peace-of-mind monitoring. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, consider a lower-priced entry product or maintain B2B focus. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a consumer proposition.. Cost: 12000 euros, 6 weeks.

Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent at $40 exceeds 30% and is at least 5 percentage points higher than at $20, indicating strong demand for peace-of-mind monitoring.; If new evidence shows that regulatory bodies in target regions actively require DIY water testing, supporting T2.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a premium, convenience-enabled solution that simplifies cleaning tasks and offers measurable time or cost savings. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently struggle with traditional cleaning methods or lack the expertise to maintain surfaces effectively.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear return on investment (e.g., reduced cleaning time, lower water usage, or increased surface longevity).. How value is captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing, subscription-based maintenance services, and data-driven upsell opportunities (e.g., suggesting accessories or upgrades).. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and performance.; The product can be distributed through existing retail channels without significant logistical changes.; Regulatory and safety standards allow consumer-grade products to be marketed as premium solutions.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offer at the same price point.; Repeat purchase rate (e.g., repeat purchase within 12 months) will be at least 10% higher for the premium product compared to a standard professional model..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a sustainable, eco-friendly solution that aligns with their environmental values and reduces water and chemical waste. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious homeowners and small business owners who prioritize sustainable cleaning practices.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from a one-time purchase to repeat purchases when they experience a clear environmental benefit (e.g., lower water usage, reduced chemical exposure, or carbon footprint reduction).. How value is captured: Tennant would capture value through premium pricing justified by sustainability credentials, partnerships with eco-friendly brands, and potential government incentives for green products.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for sustainable products.; The product can be marketed as eco-friendly without compromising performance.; Regulatory frameworks support eco-friendly cleaning product labeling and certification.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer-grade scrubber marketed as 'water‑saving' and 'chemical‑free', purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offer at the same price point.; Repeat purchase rate (e.g., repeat purchase within 12 months) will be at least 10% higher for the sustainable product compared to a standard professional model..

Test "Premium vs. Eco-Premium Consumer Scrubber Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants view a product description of a consumer-grade walk-behind scrubber (identical performance spec but marketed differently). One version is marketed as a premium convenience product (e.g., 'Save time with smart cleaning technology') and the other as an eco‑premium product (e.g., 'Water‑saving and chemical‑free cleaning solution'). Both versions are priced at a 20% premium over a comparable professional model. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 adult consumers in the US and Western Europe, screened for interest in home cleaning and willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment.. Measure: Purchase intent (1‑7 scale) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: stated importance of convenience vs. sustainability.. Predictions: T1: Premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than eco‑premium version.; T2: Eco‑premium version will achieve purchase intent at least 15% higher and higher willingness to pay than premium version.. Decision rule: If premium version purchase intent ≥ 15% points higher than eco‑premium version AND premium willingness to pay ≥ 20% higher than eco‑premium willingness to pay, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If eco‑premium version ≥ 15% points higher, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Conduct the proposed premium vs. eco‑premium conjoint test to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the premium version meets the 15‑point threshold, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition; if the eco‑premium version meets the threshold, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not yet commit to a full consumer proposition. Conduct the proposed premium vs. eco‑premium conjoint test to measure actual purchase intent and willingness to pay. If the premium version meets the 15‑point threshold, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition; if the eco‑premium version meets the threshold, develop an eco‑premium proposition. If neither meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B focus. Target customer: Homeowners and small business owners who currently struggle with traditional cleaning methods or lack the expertise to maintain surfaces effectively.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer product that delivers superior cleaning performance at an economical price point, marketed as either a premium convenience solution or an eco‑premium sustainable product, with potential for subscription services.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 8‑week, €18,000 conjoint test with 300 US/Western European consumers, comparing premium convenience vs. eco‑premium messaging.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium for cleaning equipment and the relative importance of convenience versus sustainability are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the premium version fails to achieve the 15‑point purchase intent threshold, we would abandon the consumer expansion and focus on the existing B2B segment.; If the eco‑premium version fails to achieve the 15‑point threshold, we would abandon the eco‑premium proposition and focus on premium convenience.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for a specific use case (e.g., pet‑friendly cleaning) that is not currently served, we would reconsider the consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Home consumers are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade coffee machines that offer superior taste, control, and convenience, and Franke can capture value by branding and retailing these machines directly to consumers. Who benefits: Home consumers seeking high-quality coffee experience and convenience; Franke benefits from premium pricing and direct-to-consumer margins.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of coffee quality and prosumer trend (e.g., La Marzocco Linea Micra) creates demand for machines that deliver professional results at home.. How value is captured: Franke can charge premium prices for its existing professional machines and sell them through its own channels, retaining margins rather than licensing.. Assumptions: Consumers value taste and control more than price in coffee machines.; Franke can effectively market and distribute professional machines to individual buyers.; There is sufficient demand to justify a differentiated consumer proposition.. Predictions: A survey of home coffee buyers would show >30% willing to pay at least 20% more for a machine with professional features.; Sales of Franke's existing professional machines to individual buyers would increase if positioned as premium consumer products..

T2: Home consumers are price-sensitive and prefer affordable, compact coffee solutions, so Franke should not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition but instead focus on existing professional machines and existing distribution. Who benefits: Price-sensitive home consumers seeking affordable coffee solutions; Franke benefits from maintaining its professional market and existing revenue streams.. Why behaviour changes: High price sensitivity and limited space in homes make premium professional machines less attractive to the average consumer.. How value is captured: Franke can retain margins by selling through its existing professional channels and not incurring the cost of a new consumer proposition.. Assumptions: Price is the primary barrier to purchasing home coffee machines.; Franke's existing professional machines are already well-positioned for home use.; There is no significant untapped consumer market for Franke's technology.. Test "Premium vs. Affordable Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 adult home coffee buyers (US and UK) recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and household income.. Measure: Percentage of respondents who express willingness to pay at least 20% more for a machine with professional features (premium) versus at least 20% more for an affordable, compact machine (affordable).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will choose the premium option, indicating demand for a differentiated proposition.; T2: At least 30% will choose the affordable option, indicating price sensitivity and lack of demand for a differentiated proposition.. Decision rule: If premium WTP >= 30% → proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition. If affordable WTP >= 30% → maintain focus on existing professional machines. If neither >= 30% → no expansion is justified.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, travel) with professional-grade features, rather than expanding the existing professional line. The evidence of growing premiumisation among home consumers and Franke’s existing professional machines with integrated grinders and bean-to-cup options supports this approach. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address consumer demand, pricing, or the prosumer trend that supports T1. Therefore it does not affect the theory. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home office, travel) with professional-grade features, rather than expanding the existing professional line. Target customer: Home consumers who value taste, control, and convenience in coffee, particularly those in non-commercial spaces such as offices, hospitals, and hotels.. Value proposition: Franke's existing professional machines, already equipped with integrated grinders and bean-to-cup options, can be positioned as premium consumer products offering superior coffee quality and convenience.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Premium vs. Affordable Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure willingness-to-pay for a differentiated proposition. If the premium option meets the 30% threshold, proceed with product development and branding.. Uncertainty: The exact size of the consumer market and the specific use case that will generate the most demand are uncertain. Additionally, the ability to capture premium margins without cannibalizing the professional line is unknown.. Would change if: If the test shows the affordable option meeting the 30% threshold, we would shift focus to an affordable, compact consumer proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for Franke's specific products rather than the broader premiumisation trend, we would reconsider the investment case.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a safety and peace-of-mind product, because they value personal protection and are willing to pay a premium for convenience and privacy. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking personal health protection and peace of mind.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR training as a professional or institutional requirement to a personal responsibility when they perceive it as a low-risk, private activity that can be learned at any time.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium-priced home kits, subscription-based access to training modules, and direct-to-consumer sales, leveraging its brand credibility in healthcare education.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Laerdal's medical reputation to indicate safety.; Privacy and convenience are primary purchase drivers for home health products.; Willingness to pay exceeds cost of a standard CPR kit.. T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a community or social responsibility, because they seek to contribute to public health and are motivated by peer influence and collective action. Who benefits: Individual consumers who feel a personal and social obligation to help others in cardiac emergencies.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers shift from viewing CPR training as an individual responsibility to a collective one when they see it as part of a community effort, reducing perceived risk and increasing perceived social impact.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through community-focused marketing, partnerships with schools, workplaces, and community organizations, and by offering group training programs that leverage shared responsibility.. Assumptions: Consumers are motivated by social impact and community involvement.; Peer influence and collective action increase willingness to adopt health products.; Laerdal's brand can be associated with community health initiatives effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a community-focused home CPR kit, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than for a safety-focused kit.; Surveyed consumers will rank 'helping others' as the top reason for choosing the home kit over a personal peace-of-mind kit..

Test "Home CPR Kit Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer and randomized messaging variation.. Sample: 400 US adults recruited via an online panel, screened for interest in home health products and age 25-55.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated primary reason (safety/peace-of-mind vs community/social responsibility).. Predictions: T1: Safety/peace-of-mind messaging will generate purchase intent at least 20% higher than community messaging.; T2: Community/social responsibility messaging will generate purchase intent at least 20% higher than safety/peace-of-mind messaging.. Decision rule: If safety/peace-of-mind messaging achieves purchase intent at least 20% higher than community messaging, recommend pursuing a consumer home CPR kit focused on personal protection. If community messaging achieves the higher rate, recommend a community-focused proposition. If neither meets the threshold, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes personal safety, peace of mind, and convenience, rather than community or social responsibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home CPR training that emphasizes personal safety, peace of mind, and convenience, rather than community or social responsibility. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit. Target customer: Individual consumers aged 25-55 who are interested in home health products and seek personal protection and convenience.. Value proposition: A portable, privacy-focused home CPR kit that allows learners to practice at their own pace, backed by Laerdal's medical credibility, offering peace of mind and convenience compared to classroom or professional training.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Home CPR Kit Messaging Test (400 US adults, €18,000, 10 weeks) to compare purchase intent for safety/peace-of-mind versus community messaging.. Uncertainty: The willingness to pay for a premium-priced home kit is unknown; the test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay more than a standard kit. Additionally, the competitive landscape for home CPR products is unclear.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for safety/peace-of-mind messaging at least 20% higher than for community messaging, we would shift focus to a personal-protection proposition.; If the test shows neither messaging achieving the threshold, we would recommend no expansion and continue focusing on current B2B products.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Method: Online survey with randomized messaging to test two value propositions: premium energy‑saving upgrade vs. cost‑saving long‑term investment.. Sample: 500 U.S. homeowners with central air conditioning (recruited via an online panel), stratified by household income and energy‑cost awareness.. Measure: Percentage of respondents indicating intent to purchase a Belimo smart thermostat within 12 months, and maximum price they would pay (willingness to pay).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will indicate intent to purchase if framed as a premium, energy‑saving upgrade; willingness to pay will be above €300.; T2: At least 40% will indicate intent to purchase if framed as a cost‑saving, long‑term investment; willingness to pay will be above €200.. Decision rule: If the proportion of respondents indicating intent to purchase the premium framing (T1) is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is above €300, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition. If the cost‑saving framing (T2) achieves at least 40% intent and willingness to pay above €200, also proceed. If neither condition is met, do not invest.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in regions with varying energy cost and damp/mould awareness. Participants view a product description of a Testo consumer instrument (e.g., thermal camera) and are asked to indicate their intent to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑10). The message is randomized to either energy efficiency framing (e.g, "saves heating costs, measures insulation") or health and safety framing (e.g, "detects damp, condensation, mould").. Sample: 400 homeowners (200 per condition) from regions with different average heating costs and damp/mould reports, balanced for age, gender, and income.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Energy-framed condition will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than health-framed condition, and the difference will be statistically significant (p<0.05).; T2: Health-framed condition will achieve a higher average purchase intent score than energy-framed condition, and the difference will be statistically significant (p<0.05).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for the energy-framed condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the health-framed condition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing energy efficiency. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Medical Necessity vs Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online controlled experiment with two landing pages for the same home CPR kit, each presented to a separate segment of potential consumers. Participants view the landing page for 10 seconds and are asked to indicate whether they would purchase the kit if framed as a medical necessity (T1) or as a convenient, low-cost way to learn CPR (T2). They are then asked about willingness to pay (if they would pay a premium).. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across two segments (250 per segment) to ensure random assignment. Recruitment target: individuals who have expressed interest in learning CPR for family emergencies or general health awareness.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (if they would pay a premium). Secondary: self-reported perceived importance of medical necessity versus convenience.. Predictions: T1: Segment exposed to medical necessity framing will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the convenience framing segment.; T2: Segment exposed to convenience framing will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than the medical necessity framing segment.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the medical necessity framing segment exceeds that of the convenience framing segment by at least 10 percentage points across both segments, we conclude T1 is more likely. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, we conclude neither framing significantly drives purchase intent, and we recommend further testing.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt home insulation products if they perceive them as a clear, low-effort way to reduce energy bills and improve home comfort, because they value convenience and cost savings over DIY skills. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking to lower heating costs and increase comfort without major renovations. Why behaviour changes: When the perceived benefit (energy savings) is framed as easy and direct, consumers are more likely to purchase a product they can install themselves rather than hiring professionals. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value through premium-priced direct-to-consumer sales and repeat purchases of additional insulation products. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to learn installation instructions and follow them; Energy bill reduction is a primary motivator for home insulation; Direct-to-consumer sales can reach and convert homeowners effectively. Predictions: In a survey, homeowners will report higher purchase intent when the product is marketed as 'easy DIY installation' versus a product marketed as a technical building material; Purchase intent will be higher for a product priced at a premium compared to a comparable commodity product; Repeat purchase rate will be higher for a product marketed as part of a home improvement bundle.

T2: Consumers will adopt home insulation products if they trust the product's performance and safety, because they are risk-averse and prefer products that have been tested and approved by independent bodies rather than relying on brand reputation. Who benefits: Homeowners who are concerned about product quality, safety, and long-term performance. Why behaviour changes: When a product is certified by trusted third parties (e.g., Energy Saving Trust, Building Research Establishment) and has a proven track record, consumers are more likely to purchase it even if it is priced higher. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value through premium pricing justified by certification, higher margins from quality products, and reduced return rates due to fewer installation failures. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for certified products; Certification from independent bodies is a credible signal of quality; The certification process is accessible and transparent to consumers. Predictions: In a choice experiment, consumers will select a certified product over an uncertified product even when the price difference is small; Purchase intent will be higher for a product with Energy Saving Trust certification compared to a product without certification; Repeat purchase rate will be lower for a product without certification due to higher perceived risk.

Test "DIY Installation Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase. Sample: 300 UK homeowners (150 per arm) recruited via panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each product variant. Predictions: T1: Arm A (DIY-focused, low-effort messaging) will show higher purchase intent than Arm B (certified product with premium price) by at least 10 percentage points; T2: Arm B (certified product with premium price) will show higher purchase intent than Arm A by at least 10 percentage points. Decision rule: If Arm A purchase intent >= 65% and Arm B purchase intent < 55%, conclude T1 is supported. If Arm B purchase intent >= 65% and Arm A purchase intent < 55%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither threshold is met, conclude neither theory is strongly supported (p < 0.05).. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: DIY homeowners will adopt home insulation if they perceive it as a low-cost, energy-saving upgrade that reduces their carbon footprint and monthly bills, because they value environmental responsibility and cost savings. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking to improve home energy efficiency and lower utility costs. Why behaviour changes: Environmental concerns and awareness of energy bills make them willing to invest in insulation even without professional installation.. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value by selling premium-priced insulation products directly to consumers through online channels, leveraging its existing e-commerce capabilities.. Assumptions: DIY homeowners are motivated by cost savings and environmental impact; Online purchase channels can reach these consumers effectively; Regulatory incentives (e.g., green buildings) will continue to support insulation adoption. Predictions: Consumers will purchase insulation at a price point above standard building material prices; Purchase intent will be higher among environmentally conscious households; Repeat purchases or additional accessories (e.g., windows, doors) will be more likely.

T2: Homeowners will adopt home insulation if they receive professional guidance and support, because they trust experts to ensure proper installation and compliance with building codes, reducing the risk of costly mistakes. Who benefits: Homeowners who lack DIY expertise and want a guaranteed, code-compliant result. Why behaviour changes: Professional guidance lowers perceived risk and uncertainty, making them more willing to invest in insulation even without DIY experience.. How value is captured: Kingspan can capture value by offering professional installation services, training, and support through its existing B2B channels, generating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Professional installation is perceived as more reliable than DIY; Homeowners are willing to pay a premium for expert installation; Regulatory requirements for insulation quality support professional installation. Predictions: Consumers will choose professional installation over DIY even at a higher price; Purchase intent will be higher among homeowners who have not installed insulation before; Repeat purchases of additional services (e.g., inspection, certification) will be more likely.
