Test "Digital Messaging Test: DIY vs Professional Insulation Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Run a targeted online survey with two distinct messaging paths. Recruit 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months. Randomly assign participants to one of two groups: Group A receives a DIY-focused message emphasizing cost savings, environmental impact, and ease of installation; Group B receives a professional guidance message emphasizing expert installation, code compliance, and peace of mind. Both groups are presented with a product description of Kingspan's roof insulation and a price point (e.g., £150 for a 4m² roll). Participants are asked to indicate their purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and to state the primary reason for their choice.. Sample: 1,000 UK homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and primary reason for choosing (open-ended).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and will cite cost savings and environmental impact as the primary reason.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and will cite professional guidance and code compliance as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5 - Group B average), we conclude that T1 is more supported and recommend developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on DIY motivation. If Group B's average is at least 5.5 points higher, we conclude T2 is more supported and recommend a professional guidance proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude neither theory is strongly supported and recommend further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes DIY adoption through cost savings, environmental impact, and ease of installation. Begin with a limited online pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer motivation for home insulation. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: DIY homeowners will adopt home insulation if they perceive it as a low-cost, energy-saving upgrade that reduces their carbon footprint and monthly bills, because they value environmental responsibility and cost savings.. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes DIY adoption through cost savings, environmental impact, and ease of installation. Begin with a limited online pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling. Target customer: DIY homeowners who have completed a home improvement project in the past 12 months and are looking to upgrade their home's energy efficiency.. Value proposition: Kingspan's premium-priced roof insulation sold directly to consumers via an online hub, offering clear DIY guidance, cost savings, and environmental benefits.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital Messaging Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and primary motivation. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with a full consumer launch.. Uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for insulation and the relative importance of cost savings versus professional guidance are uncertain. Regulatory changes and competition from existing DIY brands also introduce risk.. Would change if: If the pilot shows purchase intent below 3.5 out of 7 or if the primary reason is not cost savings or environmental impact, we would reconsider the DIY focus and explore professional guidance instead.; If new evidence shows strong demand for professional installation services or if regulatory barriers prevent consumer sales, we would shift focus to B2B or licensing.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1: Consumers will adopt home water testing kits because they want to monitor their drinking water quality independently and gain peace of mind, leading to repeat purchases of test strips and accessories. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and renters who are concerned about water quality but currently rely on utility or professional testing.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of water quality issues (e.g., lead, pesticides, bacteria) and a desire for control over personal health creates a willingness to invest in DIY testing.. How value is captured: Hach can capture value through recurring sales of test strips, accessories, and potentially bundled subscription services for data analysis or follow-up testing.. Assumptions: Consumers trust DIY testing results enough to act on them; Price sensitivity is manageable for a premium product; Distribution channels (hardware stores, online) are accessible to target consumers. Predictions: Willingness to pay for a premium test kit will exceed the cost of a single test; Repeat purchase rate for test strips will be higher than for one-time use; Consumer surveys will show intent to purchase a home water testing kit within the next 12 months.

Test "Segmented Messaging Test for Specialized Glove" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: 1) Specialized outdoor recreation gloves (premium, stylish positioning); 2) Specialized healthcare industrial gloves (compliance, safety positioning); 3) Standard industrial gloves (no differentiation). Each group sees its assigned message and a neutral control message. Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 1-7 scale.. Sample: 300 adult consumers (150 per segment) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect target markets.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and purchase intent on a 1-7 scale for each segment.. Predictions: T1: Specialized outdoor recreation group will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent than the standard group, indicating consumer demand for premium positioning.; T2: Specialized healthcare industrial group will show the highest average WTP and purchase intent than the standard group, indicating compliance-driven demand.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the specialized outdoor recreation group is at least 20% higher than the standard group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting outdoor recreation. If the average WTP for the specialized healthcare industrial group is at least 20% higher than the standard group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting healthcare/industrial compliance. If neither segment meets the 20% threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Differentiated Consumer Ice Machine" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from residential households in Japan. They view a mock Hoshizaki countertop ice machine with three variants: a standard compact model, a premium-priced energy-efficient model, and a basic model. Each variant is described with features such as energy rating, brand reputation, and price. Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay for each variant and whether they would purchase it.. Sample: Proposed sample: 400 Japanese residential households (200 per variant) recruited via an online panel. Recruitment target: households with at least one adult member aged 18-65 who makes purchasing decisions for home appliances.. Measure: Primary measure: average maximum price participants indicate they would pay for each variant. Secondary measure: binary purchase intent (would buy) for each variant.. Predictions: T1: Average maximum price for the standard compact variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.; T2: Average maximum price for the premium-priced variant will be the highest, and purchase intent will be low across all variants.. Decision rule: If the average maximum price for the premium-priced variant exceeds the average maximum price for the standard compact variant by at least 15% (e.g., premium price ≥ 1.15 × standard price), conclude T2 is supported and recommend a premium-priced consumer proposition. If the premium price does not exceed the standard price by 15% or if purchase intent for the premium variant is low, conclude T1 is supported and recommend a convenience-focused consumer proposition. If neither condition is met, suggest further market research.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two parallel groups. Each group views a product description of the same consumer vacuum (e.g., a compact, high‑performance machine) with either premium‑focused messaging (highlighting convenience and simplicity) or sustainability‑focused messaging (highlighting eco‑friendly features and environmental impact). Participants are then asked about willingness to pay a premium and intent to purchase.. Sample: 500 adult consumers aged 25‑55 who have purchased a vacuum cleaner in the past year, recruited via an online panel to ensure diversity in geography and demographics.. Measure: 1) Willingness to pay a premium: percentage of respondents indicating they would pay at least 20% more than the standard price. 2) Purchase intent: percentage of respondents indicating they would buy the product within the next 6 months. 3) Messaging preference: self‑reported preference for premium versus sustainability messaging.. Predictions: T1: Group receiving premium messaging will show higher willingness to pay a premium and higher purchase intent than group receiving sustainability messaging.; T2: Group receiving sustainability messaging will show higher willingness to pay a premium and higher purchase intent than group receiving premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the premium‑message group achieves at least 15% higher willingness to pay a premium and at least 10% higher purchase intent than the sustainability‑message group, proceed to develop a premium‑focused consumer proposition. If the opposite difference holds, proceed to develop a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 10% on both measures, no new proposition is recommended and the analysis is inconclusive.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is marketed as a family safety product that can be shared among relatives and friends, because they view CPR as a mutual responsibility and need to be trained together. Who benefits: Homeowners and their families gain confidence and ability to respond to cardiac arrest; Laerdal gains volume sales and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: A shift from viewing CPR training as a professional-only requirement to a shared family responsibility reduces perceived risk and increases willingness to invest in training together.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells kits directly to consumers at a premium price and can offer subscription or bundle services for family training sessions.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Laerdal's medical credibility to deliver effective training.; Family sharing motivates purchase more than individual purchase.; Regulatory or insurance incentives do not yet require home training.. Predictions: In a test offering a family-sharing kit at a premium price, purchase intent among homeowners will be at least 15% higher than a single-user kit.; Surveyed homeowners will cite 'training with family' as the top reason for choosing the product over a professional-only kit..

T2: Consumers will adopt home CPR training if it is positioned as a health insurance or employer mandate requirement, because they comply with regulatory or employer requirements rather than out of personal safety. Who benefits: Insurance companies and employers gain compliance and reduced liability; Laerdal gains volume sales through B2B contracts.. Why behaviour changes: Mandatory training shifts the decision from personal choice to compliance, making purchase easier even without personal motivation.. How value is captured: Laerdal sells kits in bulk to training centers and insurance partners, earning recurring revenue and premium margins.. Assumptions: Insurance or employer policies already require home CPR training.; Consumers will purchase to meet the mandate rather than for personal use.; Laerdal can secure contracts with insurance or HR departments.. Test "Family vs Mandate Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: Family Sharing (premium-priced kit marketed as a family safety product that can be shared among relatives and friends) or Mandate (premium-priced kit marketed as a health insurance or employer mandate requirement). Both scenarios include a brief description of the kit and a price point. Participants indicate whether they would purchase the kit and, if so, the primary reason (family sharing vs mandate).. Sample: 500 homeowners aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary reason for purchase (family sharing vs mandate).. Predictions: T1: In the Family Sharing scenario, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than in the Mandate scenario.; T2: In the Mandate scenario, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than in the Family Sharing scenario.. Decision rule: If Family Sharing purchase intent ≥ 15% and Mandate purchase intent ≤ 20%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition for family sharing. If Mandate purchase intent ≥ 20% and Family Sharing purchase intent ≤ 15%, proceed with a mandate-compliant consumer proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer market.. Cost: 18000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "DIY vs Professional Installation Choice Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase and willingness-to-pay questions. Participants are randomly assigned to either a DIY scenario (low-cost, easy installation) or a Professional scenario (guaranteed installation, premium price). Both scenarios present Kingspan's insulation product at a fixed price point (e.g., £150 for a 2m x 1m board). Participants indicate their preferred choice and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 UK homeowners (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and energy concern levels.. Measure: Primary measure: proportion of participants choosing the DIY scenario vs Professional scenario. Secondary measure: average maximum price participants would pay for each scenario.. Predictions: T1: At least 55% will choose the DIY scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.; T2: At least 55% will choose the Professional scenario and be willing to pay up to £150.. Decision rule: If DIY share ≥ 55% AND Professional share ≤ 45%, conclude T1 is supported. If Professional share ≥ 55% AND DIY share ≤ 45%, conclude T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, conclude no clear preference.. Cost: 18000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Outdoor vs Healthcare" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 outdoor recreation enthusiasts (aged 25-45, self‑identified as regular hikers, gardeners, cyclists) and 250 healthcare professionals (aged 30-55, self‑identified as nurses, doctors, or medical students) recruited via panel sites.. Measure: 1) Choice of glove type (Ansell branded vs generic) among the two groups. 2) Willingness to pay a premium (percentage points above generic price). 3) Purchase intent (yes/no) for each option.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor group will choose Ansell branded gloves and indicate higher willingness to pay a premium than healthcare group.; T2: Healthcare group will choose Ansell branded gloves and indicate higher willingness to pay a premium than outdoor group.. Decision rule: If outdoor group choice rate ≥ 60% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15 percentage points → proceed to develop outdoor‑recreation line. If healthcare group choice rate ≥ 60% and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15 percentage points → develop healthcare‑to‑consumer line. If neither group meets both thresholds → no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Value proposition: High‑performance, durable gloves designed specifically for outdoor and gardening activities, marketed as a premium, stylish solution that meets functional and aesthetic needs, allowing Ansell to capture higher margins and brand equity.. Predictions: T1: Premium Group will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay than Eco Group.; T2: Eco Group will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay than Premium Group.. Decision rule: Calculate the difference in average purchase intent scores between Premium and Eco Groups. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and their families who want to be ready for a medical emergency.. Why behaviour changes: The perceived risk of a cardiac arrest in the home increases when the threat is real, and the desire to protect loved ones motivates purchase of a product that provides immediate, easy-to-learn training.. How value is captured: Laerdal can capture value through premium pricing for a consumer-friendly kit, subscription for ongoing content, and direct-to-consumer sales that leverage existing distribution channels..
